title: F1 Score
subtitle: Topic: F1 Score · Subject: AI Evaluation and Benchmarking. Three beginner, two medium and two advanced questions, seven original diagrams, balanced answers and a tested 15-line scikit-learn example.
hero:
F1 SCORE · VISUAL STUDY

One score for the balance between precision and recall

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It counts both false alarms and missed positives, making it useful when accuracy alone overlooks important mistakes—but its averaging choices and limitations matter.

questions.stem: What does F1 Score measure in binary classification, and how do precision, recall, true positives, false positives and false negatives determine its value?
options: F1 measures overall accuracy by adding correctly predicted positives and negatives, then dividing by the total dataset size. It gives false positives and false negatives equal importance only when both classes have identical frequencies.
F1 combines precision and recall through their harmonic mean, F1=2PR/(P+R)=2TP/(2TP+FP+FN). If precision is 80% and recall is 50%, F1 is approximately 61.5%, reflecting the weaker component.
F1 is the arithmetic mean of precision and recall, so precision 80% and recall 50% produce 65%. Its purpose is to average the two scores without penalizing a large difference between them.

F1 uses the geometric mean of sensitivity and specificity to measure class balance. True negatives directly increase its numerator, so a model can achieve high positive-class F1 by correctly rejecting many negative examples.
questions.explanation: Explanation: F1 combines the correctness of positive predictions (precision) with the coverage of actual positives (recall). Its harmonic mean is 2PR/(P+R), equivalently 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN). For TP=12, FP=3 and FN=12, precision is 12/15=80% and recall is 12/24=50%. F1 is 24/39≈61.5%, lower than their 65% arithmetic average. That helps penalize a classifier that is strong on one measure but weak on the other. For example, an abuse detector needs to avoid both false accusations and missed harmful content.

For TP=12, FP=3 and FN=12, precision is 80%, recall is 50% and F1 is 24/(24+3+12)=61.5%, below their arithmetic average of 65%.

questions.tag: Beginner · F1 versus accuracy on imbalanced classes
questions.stem: Why can two classification systems have identical accuracy but very different F1 Scores, especially when one class is uncommon or operationally important?
options: F1 and accuracy must be identical whenever both models are evaluated on the same labels, because each simply counts correctly predicted examples. Differences can occur only if models use unequal test-set sizes.

F1 measures prediction confidence but ignores observed labels, while accuracy counts the labels. Two classifiers with the same accuracy differ in F1 only because their probability outputs have different calibration.

An always-negative classifier receives perfect positive-class F1 when negatives dominate, because it produces no false alarms. A second model that detects some positives necessarily has worse F1 if its accuracy is unchanged.
Accuracy counts correct predictions across both classes, while positive-class F1 focuses on TP, FP and FN. Two models can each score 80% accuracy but have F1 of 0% and 60% respectively.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Accuracy treats a correctly predicted negative as another success, even when positive events are rare. Consider 100 cases with 20 real positives. Model A predicts everything negative: it correctly rejects 80 cases, giving 80% accuracy, but positive F1 is zero because it finds no positives. Model B detects 15 positives, produces 15 false alarms and misses five positives, leaving 65 true negatives. It also achieves 80% accuracy, yet F1 is 60%. An incident-warning benchmark should report what the model actually detects, not accuracy alone.

QUESTION 02 · F1 SCORE

On 100 cases with 20 positives, predicting only negative gets 80% accuracy and F1=0. A second model gets the same accuracy but TP=15, FP=15 and FN=5, giving F1=60%.

questions.stem: How can changing a binary classifier's decision threshold alter F1 Score, and why should a threshold not be chosen using final test-set performance?
options: Changing the threshold alters the balance of false positives and false negatives, so F1 can rise or fall. Compare thresholds using validation data, then reserve a separate untouched test set for final evaluation.
Raising a threshold always increases F1 because every remaining positive prediction is more confident. The best threshold is necessarily the highest score observed in the final test predictions.

Changing a threshold adjusts the true labels in the evaluation set but does not alter predicted positive counts. Therefore precision and recall may change while F1 remains fixed for the same trained model.

A classifier must retrain its parameters for every threshold before measuring F1. The final test set can safely select the best threshold because F1 already balances false positives against missed positives.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A threshold converts probabilities into positive or negative predictions. Moving it changes TP, FP and FN, which directly changes F1. In the tested example, thresholds 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 produce F1 values of 81.5%, 75.0% and 55.6%. The highest of these demonstration scores occurs at 0.25, but that does not make it the correct production choice. Select and calibrate decisions on validation examples, taking error costs into account, and use the untouched test set only to assess the final selected system.

questions.tag: Medium · Macro, micro and weighted F1
questions.stem: How do macro, micro and support-weighted F1 Scores differ in multiclass benchmarking, and what can their disagreement reveal about rare categories?
options: Macro F1 pools all class counts before calculating one score, while micro F1 gives every class equal weight. Weighted F1 uses predicted class frequencies instead of actual support, hiding only false alarms.
All three averaging methods always equal multiclass accuracy because every example has one target label. Therefore a class with zero detected examples has no effect on the resulting F1 report.
Macro F1 averages each class's F1 equally; micro F1 pools TP, FP and FN globally; weighted F1 weights class scores by true support. Here they are 51.2%, 74.0% and 74.8%.
Macro F1 is computed by averaging precision first and recall second, then taking their harmonic mean. Micro and weighted F1 use the same operation but discard classes whose individual F1 equals zero.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In multiclass evaluation, calculate an F1 for each class by treating that class as positive. The illustrated confusion matrix gives class A F1≈81.4%, class B≈72.2%, and class C=0%. Macro F1 averages these equally, yielding 51.2%. Micro F1 pools global counts and equals 74.0%, the accuracy for this single-label multiclass task. Weighted F1 averages by each class's actual support and gives 74.8%. The gap warns that overall performance can obscure a class the model entirely misses, particularly when that class is rare.

questions.stem: How can scikit-learn calculate F1 Score on a separate test set without preprocessing leakage, while also reporting precision, recall and confusion-matrix counts?
options: Fit StandardScaler on the entire dataset before splitting, then use F1 from the training examples to choose the operating threshold. A high training F1 proves the pipeline will generalize reliably to unseen records.

Split labeled examples first, fit scaling and logistic regression inside a training pipeline, and threshold held-out class scores. Use f1_score, precision_score, recall_score and confusion_matrix on the resulting predictions.

Train a separate logistic-regression model on held-out labels for every candidate threshold and choose the one with maximum test F1. Reusing the test set is unbiased because no training labels are changed.

Calculate F1 by averaging the predicted class probabilities without consulting true labels. A classifier's calibration and its F1 are interchangeable, so no confusion matrix or held-out evaluation is necessary.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The included 15-line scikit-learn script creates 260 labeled synthetic cases and splits them into 195 training and 65 test examples. Its Pipeline fits StandardScaler and LogisticRegression using training data only. It then obtains positive-class scores for the holdout and applies three fixed thresholds. The confusion matrix supplies TP, FP, FN and TN; f1_score, precision_score and recall_score evaluate each decision set. The measured F1 values are 0.815, 0.750 and 0.556. In a real selection workflow, tune the threshold on validation data before testing.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · F1 SCORE
scikit-learn · F1 at three thresholds 15 lines
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, f1_score, precision_score, recall_score
X,y=make_classification(n_samples=260,n_features=6,n_informative=4,
    n_redundant=0,weights=[.80,.20],flip_y=.025,class_sep=1.1,random_state=37)
Xtr,Xte,ytr,yte=train_test_split(X,y,test_size=.25,stratify=y,random_state=13)
model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)).fit(Xtr,ytr)
scores=model.predict_proba(Xte)[:,1]
for threshold in (.25,.50,.75):
    pred=(scores>=threshold).astype(int)
    tn,fp,fn,tp=confusion_matrix(yte,pred).ravel()
    print(threshold,(tp,fp,fn,tn),round(f1_score(yte,pred),3),round(precision_score(yte,pred,zero_division=0),3),round(recall_score(yte,pred),3))

A training-only scaler and logistic-regression model evaluate 65 unseen cases. The tested code reports confusion counts and F1 values of 0.815, 0.750 and 0.556 for three thresholds.

questions.stem: Why can sample-averaged F1 differ from micro-averaged and macro-averaged F1 in multilabel classification, and how should a benchmark interpret these different views?
options: Sample-averaged F1 treats the entire dataset as one global confusion matrix, while micro F1 averages class metrics equally. The two can differ only when examples have different numerical feature scales.

Sample-averaged F1 divides the number of exactly matching label sets by the number of examples, while micro F1 counts partially correct labels. Thus sample F1 is identical to exact-match accuracy by definition.

Sample, micro and macro F1 must all coincide if each example can have multiple true labels, because labels are independent. Choosing an averaging method matters only for regression or mutually exclusive multiclass problems.

Sample-averaged F1 calculates each example's label-set F1 before averaging, micro F1 pools all label decisions, and macro F1 averages per-label scores equally. The illustrated results are 45.8%, 54.5% and 50.0%.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Multilabel examples can have several correct labels simultaneously, so the unit of averaging matters. Samples F1 calculates an F1 for the predicted and true label sets of each example, then averages across examples. Micro F1 pools TP, FP and FN across all labels, while macro F1 averages a separate score for each label. For the four illustrated examples, samples F1 is about 45.8%, micro F1 about 54.5%, and macro F1 50.0%. This matters in image tagging, where partially correct tags should not automatically count as an exact match.

questions.tag: Advanced · F-beta, zero division and trustworthy benchmarking
questions.stem: When might F1 Score be insufficient for AI evaluation, and how do F-beta weighting, zero-division conventions and proper validation improve benchmark interpretation?
options: F1 weights precision and recall equally, but applications may prioritize one error type; F-beta can shift that emphasis. Declare zero-division handling, report class support, and select thresholds without using final test outcomes.

F1 should replace every metric when positive examples are rare because its harmonic mean automatically expresses the true business cost of each error. F-beta and per-class reporting therefore add no useful information.

F-beta changes the number of ground-truth positives rather than the relative importance of precision and recall. Its scores are unbiased even when thresholds are repeatedly chosen from the final evaluation dataset.

Zero-division cases should be assigned perfect F1 because the model avoided false positives. Calibration, class prevalence and the false-positive versus false-negative costs do not affect how useful F1 is in deployment.
questions.explanation: Explanation: F1 combines precision and recall symmetrically, but the harm from false alarms and missed positives may differ. F-beta allows a different emphasis: beta greater than one favors recall, while beta below one favors precision. With precision 80% and recall 50%, F0.5≈71.4%, F1≈61.5%, and F2≈54.1%. When both predictions and ground truth contain no positives, F1 is mathematically undefined and reporting depends on the chosen zero_division convention. Report support and error counts, tune on validation data, and preserve an untouched test set.
